target_audience: University students (Calculus/Linear Algebra) or advanced high school students

sections.title: Shift in Perspective: From Slope to Scaling
lecture_lines: We usually view derivatives as slopes on a graph.
But derivatives also describe how functions stretch space.
This is known as the transformational view of derivatives.
animations: Display a 2D coordinate system with a white (#FFFFFF) curve and a yellow (#FFFF00) tangent line at a point.
Morph the 2D graph into a single horizontal white (#FFFFFF) number line.
Introduce a red (#FF0000) box labeled 'Stretching Machine' above the line.
Animate a cyan (#00FFFF) segment on the line passing through the machine and becoming longer.
Highlight a specific point in yellow (#FFFF00) and show a 'Scale: 2x' label.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Linear Transformations on 1D Space
lecture_lines: Consider a simple linear transformation like y equals mx.
The constant m acts as a uniform scaling factor.
It stretches or squashes the entire input number line.
animations: Create a horizontal white (#FFFFFF) line with tick marks at integers 0, 1, 2.
Animate the line expanding so the distance between ticks triples.
Add a yellow (#FFFF00) label 'm = 3' and the text 'Constant Scaling Factor'.

sections.title: The 'Zoom' Effect: Local Linearity
lecture_lines: Globally, most functions appear curved and complex.
However, zooming in at a point reveals local linearity.
At this tiny scale, the function looks like a line.
The derivative represents the scaling factor at this spot.
It tells us how local space is being transformed.
animations: Draw a white (#FFFFFF) parabolic curve y = x^2 on a black background.
Place a small red (#FF0000) dot (Micro-Ant) at the point (2, 4).
Scale the view up 10x, centered on the red dot, until the curve is a straight line.
Draw a cyan (#00FFFF) horizontal arrow dx and a magenta (#FF00FF) vertical arrow dy.
Show the text 'dy = 4 * dx' in yellow (#FFFF00) next to the arrows.

sections.title: Visualizing the Transformation: The Dual Number Line
lecture_lines: Imagine two parallel lines representing input and output.
Arrows map points from the input to the output.
Watch a tiny change, dx, on the input line.
This results in a corresponding change, dy, on output.
The ratio dy over dx is the local stretch.
animations: Display two parallel white (#FFFFFF) horizontal lines labeled 'Input X' and 'Output Y'.
Draw cyan (#00FFFF) arrows connecting points x on Input to y = sin(x) on Output.
Create a small cyan (#00FFFF) interval dx = 0.1 on the Input line.
Show the corresponding magenta (#FF00FF) interval dy on the Output line.
Pulse both intervals and display 'Ratio dy/dx = 1' in yellow (#FFFF00).

sections.title: The Formal Transformation Formula
lecture_lines: We can formalize this using the transformation formula.
The change dy equals the derivative times dx.
Here, the derivative acts as a linear map.
It transforms input displacement into output displacement.
This view generalizes easily to higher dimensions.
animations: Present the formula df = f'(x) * dx in large white (#FFFFFF) text.
Transform the formula into df = 6 * dx using yellow (#FFFF00) for the '6'.
Show a short cyan (#00FFFF) vector dx being scaled into a magenta (#FF00FF) vector df six times longer.

sections.title: Conclusion: Why This Matters
lecture_lines: This perspective is vital for multivariable calculus.
It treats derivatives as matrices transforming space.
Think of derivatives as local growth settings for functions.
animations: Display a white (#FFFFFF) 2D grid that warps and stretches locally.
Fade in a yellow (#FFFF00) slider icon labeled 'Local Growth Setting'.
Fade out all elements and show 'Derivatives = Local Scaling' in white (#FFFFFF).
